clue.text: Rank Keith last in project, without further ado

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters inside the word for project

parts.note: to project is to jut out

indicators.note: rank in the sense of arranging in rows, so the letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Keith comes bottom of the rankings in a school project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like a noun or adjective but rearranges KEITH and LAST into STLIKETHA, which goes 'in' JUT ('project').
explanation.definitionFit: The catchphrase of magician Tommy Cooper, it means immediately and with no fuss or preamble.

clue.text: Night-time suits block by modernist architect

parts.note: a jam is a block — traffic that will not move is jammed
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the last director of the Bauhaus and the man behind the Seagram Building, is known by his middle name alone

explanation.surface: Darkness flattering an apartment block put up by a famous modernist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits' is a verb in the surface — night-time suits the building — and a plural noun in the answer. Mies van der Rohe is always just Mies once the wordplay has him.
explanation.definitionFit: Jammies is the nursery shortening of pyjamas, the loose two-piece suit worn in bed.

clue.text: Species of small tortoise seen in odd places to the north

indicators.note: Letters seen in odd places are the first, third, fifth and seventh, so every other letter of the word is stepped over.
North is up the page, so in a down entry everything gathered so far is read from the bottom back up to the top.

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for small, as on a clothing label
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of TORTOISE

explanation.surface: A small tortoise species recorded at scattered sites further north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Species' is the everyday sense of kinds, not the biological rank the tortoise dangles in front of you. Everything collected is turned round in one go, so the abbreviation ends up at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorts are kinds or varieties — all sorts of people — which is what species means outside the laboratory.

clue.text: Field sets off with half dropping out

indicators.note: Half of something dropping out leaves the other half behind, so a six-letter word arrives with only its first three letters.

parts.note: a train that sets off leaves, and the last three letters drop away

explanation.surface: A race field starting out with half the entrants withdrawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Field' is the runners in a race in the surface and grazing land in the answer. Lea is Gray's word in the Elegy — the lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is an open stretch of grassland or meadow, a field left to pasture.

clue.text: Picture card Welshman turned up after king

indicators.note: Turning something up in a down entry means writing it from the bottom towards the top, so the name is read backwards.

parts.note: k is the letter on the king in both chess and cards

indicators.note: What comes after the king is written below him in a down entry, so his letter heads the answer.

parts.note: Evan is the Welsh form of John and the standard crossword Welshman

explanation.surface: A Welshman showing up only once the king has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived and instructs you to write the name the other way round. Knave is the older name for the card now usually called the jack.
explanation.definitionFit: The knave is the court card ranking between the ten and the queen, one of the three picture cards in each suit.

clue.text: Scrape lady's underwear with Marmite?

parts.note: tights are the close-fitting legwear worn under a skirt
a marmite is a big lidded stewpot, the French word the yeast spread took its name from — there is one drawn on the label

explanation.surface: A jar of Marmite being scraped across a lady's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the brand name is being read as the ordinary French kitchen word behind it. 'Scrape' is the definition and does none of the scraping the surface pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight spot is a fix with no room to manoeuvre in, which is what a scrape means when you are in one.

clue.text: American colourist upset East European periodically

parts.note: a is the dictionary abbreviation for American
someone who tints things is a tinter

indicators.note: Upset means turned over, and a word turned over in a down entry is written from its last letter up to its first.

parts.note: the Slavs are the East European peoples — Poles, Czechs, Serbs, Russians

explanation.surface: An American colourist getting an East European annoyed every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' is the word to watch: it usually tells you to take every second letter, and here it is the definition. 'Upset' reads as annoyed and means write it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done at intervals happens with gaps between the doings, which is what periodically describes.

clue.text: E.g. Christie's produce etchings, lithographs, etc in series

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for series, the S of S1 E1
etchings and lithographs are prints, and a printer is what produces them

explanation.surface: An auction house bringing out a sale of prints one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: Christie's the auction house is a front for Linford Christie, the Olympic hundred-metres champion. Etchings and lithographs are both kinds of print, which is what delivers the printer.
explanation.definitionFit: Linford Christie won the 100 metres at the 1992 Olympics, so he is one example of a sprinter — a runner over the short distances.

clue.text: Eggs sat on by considerate male penguin

indicators.note: Whatever sits on something is above it, so in a down entry the sitter is written first and what he sits on goes underneath.

parts.note: a gent is a man, and the courtesy is built into the word
two eggs drawn as two O's

explanation.surface: A thoughtful male penguin taking his turn on the eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: Male penguins really do incubate, so the picture is natural history rather than nonsense. The gentoo is the one with the orange bill and the white flash over the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The gentoo is one of the brush-tailed penguins of the Antarctic and the sub-Antarctic islands, so penguin names its family.

clue.text: Nougat confection cooked with sweet wine

parts.note: a Mars bar is nougat and caramel under chocolate
on a menu a la is the French for done in the style of, as in a la creme

explanation.surface: A nougat dessert simmered in a sweet wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like an anagram instruction and is half of a menu tag instead. Marsala comes from the Sicilian town of that name and is what zabaglione is made with.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsala is the fortified wine of western Sicily, drunk sweet after dinner and used in the kitchen.

clue.text: Catch sight of naughty kid cutting legs off

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the child goes inside the other letters
off in the sense of gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
an imp is a mischievous child

explanation.surface: A naughty child chopping the legs off something, perhaps a doll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'legs off' reads as amputation, but 'off' rearranges LEGS into GLSE, and IMP is 'cutting' into it.
explanation.definitionFit: To glimpse something is to see it briefly, which is what catching sight of it means.

clue.text: Popular figure out with conservationists on the rocks

parts.note: what is popular is in, as in fashion
to figure something out is to solve it
NT is the National Trust, the charity that owns great stretches of the British coast and countryside

explanation.surface: A celebrity spending the day out among the rocks with conservationists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular figure' reads as one phrase and is torn in two by the wordplay, which takes the verb 'figure out' instead. On the rocks is where a ship ends up as well as a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A business on the rocks has run aground and cannot pay, which is what insolvent says of it in the accountant's word.

clue.text: Act is fool's last during diplomatic mission

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so these letters are dropped into the middle of the word named after.

parts.note: a legation is a diplomatic mission ranking below an embassy
the word is taken as it stands
the last letter of FOOL

explanation.surface: A fool's final turn during a diplomatic visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' is the parliamentary kind, not the performance the fool is putting on. A legation is the smaller sort of embassy, headed by a minister rather than an ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: Legislation is law as parliament makes it, and a single Act of Parliament is one piece of it.

clue.text: Wind noodle around middle of chopstick

indicators.note: What goes around something is wrapped right round it, so the letter named next sits inside.

parts.note: a noodle is a fool, and so is a twit
chopstick has nine letters, so it has one letter in the middle

explanation.surface: Noodles being wound round the middle of a chopstick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noodle' is the supper in the surface and an old word for a fool in the wordplay, which is what makes the chopstick look innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind a wire round a post is to twist it, so wind and twist are the same verb.

clue.text: Doubtfully lift pipe down by carpet

parts.note: sh is the noise you make when you are telling someone to pipe down
a rug is a small carpet

explanation.surface: Somebody hesitantly lifting a pipe that runs down beside the carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipe down' is plumbing in the surface and a demand for quiet in the wordplay. What gets lifted in the answer is a pair of shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: To shrug is to raise the shoulders, and the gesture says you neither know nor care — the doubt is part of the word.

clue.text: Bruce Willis film that's bagged an Oscar released

indicators.note: To bag a thing is to put it in the bag, so what the film bagged is shut up inside the film's title.

parts.note: Red, the 2010 action comedy with Willis as a retired CIA man
Oscar Wilde — the first name points at the man, the surname supplies the letters

explanation.surface: A Bruce Willis picture that picked up an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: Films bag Oscars all the time, which is exactly what hides the fact that this Oscar is a person. Rewilding is the conservation business of putting land or animals back to the wild.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal that has been rewilded has been let out of captivity and back into the wild, so released covers it.

clue.text: Water bus manoeuvring at stop-over loses seconds

indicators.note: manoeuvring means moving about, so the letters are shifted into a new order
loses means some letters go missing from the pool before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A bus manoeuvring at a stopover is losing time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvring' acts on AT STOP-OVER, which 'loses' S (seconds), so ATTOPOVER is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaporetto is a motorboat serving as public transport on the canals of Venice.

clue.text: Fiddle turned into crime

parts.note: a viola is a stringed instrument of the fiddle family

indicators.note: turned means changed around, so the letters of the short word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A minor fiddle that grew into a full-blown crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' suggests fraud, but it is the instrument; INTO is 'turned' into TION.
explanation.definitionFit: A violation is a breach of a law or rule, so it can mean an offence.

clue.text: Seaside town bluer than any other, frequently

parts.note: to feel blue is to feel low, so the bluest of the lot is the lowest
oft is the old short form of often

explanation.surface: A resort gloomier than anywhere else on the coast, and gloomy time after time.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue and low are the same word for misery, so the superlative of one is the superlative of the other. Lowestoft is the Suffolk fishing port that is the most easterly town in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowestoft is a fishing port and holiday resort on the Suffolk coast, sat on the North Sea.

clue.text: Klutz left masseur without top

indicators.note: without its top means the first letter is taken off the word

parts.note: a masseur rubs clients, so is a rubber

explanation.surface: A clumsy person walked out on by a masseur with no shirt on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like a verb but is L; RUBBER (masseur) goes 'without top', losing its R.
explanation.definitionFit: A lubber is a big clumsy oaf, as in landlubber, so it matches a klutz.

clue.text: Missile part thinned with file

indicators.note: thinned means pared down, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: the word part without its first and last letters
a file is a row, a line of people or things

explanation.surface: A component of a missile has been thinned down using a metal file.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' looks like a component of the missile, but 'thinned' strips it to AR; ROW ('file') follows 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow is a projectile shot from a bow, an early kind of missile.

clue.text: How exhilarating to go flat out for stunt

parts.note: whee is the cry you let out on the way down a helter-skelter
to go flat out is to lie stretched on the ground

explanation.surface: Somebody thrilled at the thought of travelling at top speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat out' means at full speed in the surface and stretched on the floor in the wordplay, and the swap is the whole clue. A wheelie is riding along on the back wheel with the front one in the air.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheelie is the trick of lifting a bike's front wheel and riding on the back one, which is a stunt.

clue.text: Learner in Saab bumped tree

indicators.note: A car that has been bumped has been knocked out of shape, and so have these letters.

parts.note: the L-plate a British learner driver has to display
four more letters for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A learner driver putting a Saab into a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The prang is the anagram — 'bumped' does to the letters what it does to the car. Balsa is the featherweight wood that model aeroplanes are built from.
explanation.definitionFit: The balsa is a fast-growing tropical American tree, cut for the lightest timber in commercial use.

clue.text: Heavens, how quickly a chocolate bar goes

parts.note: an Aero is the bubbly British chocolate bar, and the answer wants it possessive — a chocolate bar's
the pace of a thing is how quickly it goes

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the speed a bar of chocolate disappears.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is doing the joining: the speed at which an Aero goes is that bar's pace. 'Heavens' is the cry of astonishment and the definition at the same time.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerospace is the earth's atmosphere and the space beyond it taken together, which is the heavens as an engineer divides them up.

clue.text: Department concerned with charitable donations, mostly

parts.note: re means regarding, concerned with

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: alms are gifts to the poor

explanation.surface: A government department that deals with most charitable giving.
explanation.walkthrough: RE ('concerned with') is followed by ALMS, cut 'mostly' to ALM.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm can mean a field or sphere of activity, as in 'the realm of science', like a department.

clue.text: Bewildered when temperature rises in a constituency

indicators.note: temperature is T, and in a down entry rising means moving up, so the T moves to the front

parts.note: a seat is a parliamentary constituency

explanation.surface: A district gets flustered when the weather heats up.
explanation.walkthrough: A SEAT ('a constituency'): in this down entry its T ('temperature') 'rises' from the bottom to sit just after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at sea is an idiom for being confused and lost, like a sailor without bearings.

clue.text: I wear myself out in retirement, like some professors perhaps

indicators.note: To be in retirement is to have gone back, and letters that have gone back are read from the end to the start.

parts.note: the speaker of the clue, taken as the letter
to wear myself out is to tire me

explanation.surface: Somebody exhausting themselves even after giving up work.
explanation.walkthrough: Retirement is both what the professors have taken and the instruction to read the wordplay backwards. Emeriti is the Latin plural — one such professor is emeritus.
explanation.definitionFit: Professors who have retired but keep their chair's title are emeriti, so the answer names precisely that group.

clue.text: In a deep depression, covered with baby's saliva

indicators.note: What is covered lies under what covers it, so the answer is buried in the words that follow.

parts.note: the run starts on the second letter of the first word and stops three letters into the second, stepping over the apostrophe and the space as if neither were there

explanation.surface: Somebody thoroughly miserable and covered in a baby's dribble.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is stepped over as though it were not there, which is what keeps the buried word out of sight. Abyssal is the zone of the ocean below about four thousand metres.
explanation.definitionFit: The abyssal zone is the deep ocean floor, so abyssal describes whatever lies far down in a trough.

clue.text: Extras denied lead part, I suppose

indicators.note: Denied the leading part means refused the front, so the word loses its first letter.

parts.note: in cricket a bye is one of the extras, a run scored when the ball beats bat and wicketkeeper alike

explanation.surface: Bit-part actors turned down for the starring role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extras' are the crowd on a film set in the surface and cricket's extras in the wordplay — the byes, leg byes and wides that are not scored off the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: I suppose is the grudging assent you offer when you mean yes without any enthusiasm for it.

clue.text: Simple penniless fellow returned, with money in pockets? Certainly

parts.note: and means with, along with

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Simple Simon of the nursery rhyme, who told the pieman he had not any money
the take is the money taken in, the takings that go into the pockets

explanation.surface: A naive broke man comes home with a pocketful of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Simple Simon wanted a pie but had no penny; his name 'returned' gives NOMIS. AND ('with') leads, and TAKE (takings) ends.
explanation.definitionFit: And no mistake is an emphatic tag meaning without doubt, the sense of surely.
